summary: Analyzes how the number of label switched paths scales in MPLS-TE core networks, and examines two techniques, LSP hierarchies and multipoint-to-point LSPs, for improving scale. It aims to motivate better deployment techniques. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: If a network has too many separate private roads, it gets hard to keep track of them all. This memo studies how big the problem gets and ways to shrink it.

questions: how many lsps can an mpls-te network support
how do lsp hierarchies reduce lsp count
subtitle: Strategies for supporting thousands of label-switched paths in core networks

tldr.problem: MPLS-TE networks need to support full connectivity between thousands of edge routers, which creates thousands of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that must be tracked and managed at core routers, risking memory exhaustion and control-plane overload.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes two network topologies (snowflake and ladder), calculates LSP counts at each level, and examines two techniques—hierarchical LSP tunnels and multipoint-to-point LSPs—that reduce the number of paths core routers must handle directly.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can plan large MPLS-TE deployments by understanding the scaling limits and choosing appropriate topology designs and LSP aggregation strategies, though trade-offs exist between scaling and cost-efficiency.

today: RFC 5439 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It provides guidance to operators planning large MPLS-TE deployments and motivates the development of deployment techniques and protocol extensions to enable scaling.

sections.title: The MPLS-TE Scaling Challenge
sections.content:
MPLS-TE (Traffic Engineering) is a technology that creates explicit, managed paths called Label Switched Paths (LSPs) between any pair of edge routers in a network. It allows operators to control traffic flows and ensure quality of service.

However, as networks grow to support thousands of edge routers (often called Provider Edge or PE routers), the problem emerges that every edge router wants an LSP to every other edge router—creating a full mesh of LSPs. This means core routers must track, maintain, and forward data along tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of paths, limited only by router memory and processing power. This RFC analyzes whether existing protocols and routers can handle networks of the size operators need.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TE is like having a traffic controller that knows exactly where each delivery should go. But when you have thousands of trucks, the controller has to remember thousands of routes, which gets hard.

sections.title: The Scaling Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four main concerns that limit MPLS-TE networks:

LSP state: Each LSP requires memory to store its forwarding and control-plane information at every router it traverses. When a router must maintain state for tens of thousands of LSPs, memory capacity becomes the limiting factor.

Processing overhead: Routers must search through their control blocks to find the right forwarding state for each incoming packet. As the number of LSPs grows, search times increase and can eventually degrade performance.

RSVP-TE soft-state refresh: RSVP-TE, the signaling protocol for MPLS-TE, periodically sends refresh messages to maintain state. With thousands of LSPs, refresh traffic can overwhelm the control plane. Observations suggest that routers struggle above 50,000 LSPs.

Management limitations: The tools and protocols used to provision and monitor LSPs often have practical limits. Network management systems may be swamped by requests to read information about thousands of LSPs.
sections.eli5: Keeping track of thousands of routes takes memory, makes the router slower, creates too many status messages, and makes it hard to manage.

sections.title: Network Topology Models
sections.content:
The RFC examines two generic network topologies that represent real deployments:

Snowflake topology: A small, fully meshed core of P(1) nodes (core routers), with tree-shaped branches hanging off it. Multiple levels of intermediate routers (P(2), P(3), etc.) build a hierarchy down to the edge PEs. This is common in networks with abundant fiber connectivity.

Ladder topology: A long, thin core shaped like a ladder, with two parallel spars (main lines) connected by rungs (cross-connections). Trees of edge routers hang off the spars. This model suits geographically stretched networks.

For each topology, the RFC parameterizes networks by the number of nodes and connectivity multipliers at each level, then calculates how many LSPs must pass through each node. In both topologies, unmanaged flat networks create unacceptably high LSP counts at core nodes—for a 1,000-PE network, core nodes might see over 300,000 LSPs.
sections.eli5: Real networks are shaped either like snowflakes with a meshed core and tree branches, or like ladders with two main lines connected by rungs. The shape matters for how many routes end up at each router.

sections.title: Improving Scale with Hierarchical LSPs
sections.content:
LSP hierarchies use Forwarding Adjacencies (FAs)—LSP tunnels that act as logical links. The core routers establish a mesh of FA tunnels between intermediate nodes, and edge-to-edge LSPs are tunneled inside these FAs.

For example, in a snowflake network, routers at level P(2) establish a full mesh of FA tunnels to each other. All PE-to-PE LSPs are tunneled inside these P(2) FAs, so the top-level P(1) nodes no longer see individual PE-to-PE LSPs—they only see the P(2)-to-P(2) FAs. This dramatically reduces the number of LSPs at the core from hundreds of thousands to hundreds.

A three-level hierarchy can be even more effective. The trade-off is that the network needs more intermediate routers and more careful configuration to set up the mesh groups. Additionally, the technique does not reduce the LSP count at the level of routers closest to the PEs, only at higher levels.
sections.eli5: Instead of each delivery having its own route, group them into super-routes. Thousands of deliveries go through a handful of super-routes, so the controller only tracks the super-routes.

sections.title: Multipoint-to-Point LSPs and Combined Approaches
sections.content:
Another technique mentioned is Multipoint-to-Point (MP2P) LSPs, where multiple sources send traffic to a single destination over a shared tree. This reduces the total number of LSPs needed because instead of every source-destination pair having a separate path, sources share paths toward their destination.

The RFC also discusses combined models where hierarchies and MP2P approaches are used together, and an alternative approach based on different network structure assumptions. Each technique has merits and drawbacks: hierarchies solve the core problem but add configuration complexity; MP2P LSPs reduce overall LSP count but require different semantics and operational procedures.

The RFC concludes that no single technique is optimal for all scenarios and that operators must balance scaling requirements against cost-effectiveness and operational complexity.
sections.eli5: You can also have multiple trucks send their deliveries along one shared road, instead of each having its own. Or you can mix both ideas together.
